parent_context.title: Walking policy won't start slow walk from stand still
parent_context.text:
Hi! I've been setting up `duck-sim` and noticed the duck wouldn't walk when I asked for a slow walk. It just stands there. I dug in a bit and I think it's the shipped v5 policies rather than anything in the runtime.

From a standstill, both `alpha_walking.onnx` and `velstand.onnx` refuse to take a step below about 0.22 m/s, even though training samples `lin_vel_x` from `(-0.4, 0.4)`. What surprised me is that it happens in the training env too. I ran the ONNX in `Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck` with a pinned twist command (32 envs, mean forward speed in m/s):

| cmd vx | play cfg as is | play cfg, pushes off | `velstand`, pushes off |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.15 | 0.078 | **0.007** (1/32 walking) | **0.002** (0/32) |
| 0.20 | – | 0.071 (10/32) | 0.021 (1/32) |
| 0.30 | 0.146 | 0.144 | 0.141 |

I think the reason nobody's caught it is that in-sim play pushes the robot every 0.5–1.0 s, and each push nudges it into stepping. So in play it looks fine. Once it's moving it'll happily keep going at 0.15. It just can't *start* slow. I see the same thing in `scripts/infer_policy.py` and through `robotd --sim`, so it doesn't look like a sim2sim gap.

It feels related to #46, but this one is about the policies people are running right now.

A few ideas, in case they're useful:

- **Evaluate with pushes off.** The export/publish check, or a quick play mode, could command a slow speed from rest with pushes disabled, so this shows up before a set ships.
- **Look at the forward-only share.** The base cfg has `rel_forward_envs=0.2` with forward-only commands clamped to `vx >= 0.3`, so a chunk of training never sees slow forward walking. I haven't verified this is the cause, though.
- **More episodes starting at rest.** Episodes that begin from a standstill with a small nonzero command would teach it to break into a walk at low speed.


Tested on `develop` @ `cb70b79`, `seed-v5`
parent_context.author: wengmister

text:
Adding numbers from a client driving the policies through `robot.move` in the full simulator (apartment scene, official policies), since two of them aren't in the tables above:

- **Turning in place**: the threshold sits around **1.1 rad/s** commanded; below it the duck doesn't step. Between the 0.8 (no) and 1.5 (yes) points above.
- **Real vs commanded**: 0.22 m/s commanded → ~0.09 m/s; 0.30 → ~0.13 m/s; 1.4 rad/s → 0.65–0.97 rad/s.
- **Drift**: walking straight at 0.26–0.30 m/s commanded, it veers **right by 35–50° in 8 s**.

How a client copes in the meantime, in case it helps others: command at least 0.24 m/s / 1.4 rad/s, measure turns on `odom.yaw` instead of timing them (a timed turn comes out at roughly half the angle), and close a small PI loop on `odom.yaw` while walking straight to cancel the drift. Code: https://github.com/samoxis/microduck-brain (`config.py` thresholds, `brain.py` heading hold).

parent_context.title: apartment scene: ToF beams into the stairwell pass under the floor slab and read "no target"
parent_context.text:
In `scene_apartment.xml` the stairwell (x ∈ [-0.40, 0.00], y ∈ [-1.40, -0.70]) has steps but no walls or bottom, and the floors around it are 1 cm slabs over empty space. A downward ToF beam that enters the hole at a shallow angle misses the steps, passes under the slab beyond, and hits nothing — so `sim/tof.py` reports status 255 ("nothing in range") where a real VL53L8CX would measure the stairwell's wall or bottom.

Repro, sensor at standing height over the north corridor, looking south:

```python
import numpy as np, mujoco
m = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path("src/mjlab_microduck/robot/microduck/scene_apartment.xml")
d = mujoco.MjData(m); mujoco.mj_forward(m, d)
g = np.zeros(1, dtype=np.int32)
for el in (8.4, 14.1, 19.7):                      # rows 5-7 of the 8x8 grid, head level
    e = np.radians(el); v = np.array([0, -np.cos(e), -np.sin(e)])
    print(el, mujoco.mj_ray(m, d, np.array([-0.2, -0.25, 0.246]), v, None, 1, -1, g))
# 8.4 -> 1.657 (floor beyond the hole)   14.1 -> -1.0   19.7 -> -1.0
```

Why it matters: a cliff guard developed in the simulator only ever sees the "nothing in range" signature of a drop; on the robot it would see a longer range instead. Both should be handled, but only one can be tested here.

A possible fix, five boxes lining the hole 0.6 m deep:

```xml
<geom name="well_bottom" type="box" size="0.20 0.35 0.005" pos="-0.20 -1.05 -0.605"/>
<geom name="well_n" type="box" size="0.20 0.005 0.30" pos="-0.20 -0.695 -0.30"/>
<geom name="well_s" type="box" size="0.20 0.005 0.30" pos="-0.20 -1.405 -0.30"/>
<geom name="well_w" type="box" size="0.005 0.35 0.30" pos="-0.405 -1.05 -0.30"/>
<geom name="well_e" type="box" size="0.005 0.35 0.30" pos="0.005 -1.05 -0.30"/>
```

With them the same beams read 1.186 m and 1.221 m (the south wall). Checked against `develop` @ 8d0db74 with MuJoCo directly; I haven't run the full training or the policies with the change.

Found while building a drop detector for an autonomy client: https://github.com/samoxis/microduck-brain (fixtures with these frames in `tests/fixtures/mujoco_drop.json`).
parent_context.author: samoxis

text: Confirmed the root cause: `src/mjlab_microduck/robot/microduck/apartment.xml` builds the stair steps and side corridor slabs but no collision geometry for the well itself, so shallow-angle ToF rays (`src/mjlab_microduck/sim/tof.py:26`, `STATUS_NO_TARGET=255`) pass under the floor. I reproduced it locally with mujoco.mj_ray (14.1°/19.7° -> -1) and will submit a fix adding the five well boxes (bottom + n/s/w/e walls) at the positions proposed above, plus a small CPU-only regression test. Reproduced with AI assistance; the fix and test are written by me (AI-assisted, disclosed per repo norms).

STLs in `assets/` are decimated (`simplify_stls: true`) — fine for MuJoCo, not great for parts that need to mate with a real XL330 servo or the HAT board. The Onshape source linked in `config_mjcf_allcollisions.json` is private, so there's no way to get real CAD precision for printing right now.

Separately: meshes export in meters with no `scale` on the MJCF `<mesh>` tags, so anyone slicing these needs a 1000x scale-up first. Worth a one-line README note.

Any chance of STEP exports for the printable parts, or making the Onshape doc link-shareable? Models are already CC BY-SA-NC, so this fits the spirit.

title: Community port: training the walking task on AMD GPUs (ROCm) via Genesis
timestamp_note: 缺失时间保持null；项目说明不把仓库更新时间当正文更新时间
classification_basis: 待人工归类；官方参考仓库和独立讨论不强行计作第三方项目

parent_context.title: Community port: training the walking task on AMD GPUs (ROCm) via Genesis
parent_context.text: Hi, The README notes that training requires a CUDA GPU, since it runs through MuJoCo Warp. For people on AMD hardware there is now an alternative: I ported the walking task to the Genesis simulator, which runs on ROCm. https://github.com/Macmachi/microduck-rl-genesis The aim was to carry your sim2real recipe across rather than invent another one. Preserved value for value: the BAM M6 actuator fitted for the XL330 (firmware voltage law, DC torque, and the Coulomb/Stribeck/load-dependent friction budget written into `dof_frictionloss` so that the solver performs the static clipping, as in BAM algorithm 1), the 61-D observation contract, the reward weights, the domain randomisation ranges and the curricula, each value keeping the comment that explains it. Rewritten, because it depends on `mujoco_warp` or on mjlab's managers: the actuator implementation, the environment class, the sensors, the rough terrain (height field instead of stacked boxes) and the ONNX export. A port is only worth its checks, so the repository ships them: - the actuator is run against MuJoCo + BAM on the same robot, the same actuator and the same initial state (maximum torque deviation 3.2e-9 N·m) - the formulas are compared directly against Rhoban/bam - the deployment chain is tested end to end: the exported ONNX replays the policy on real episode observations rather than on synthetic vectors (under 1e-6 rad over 60 steps) The limits, stated plainly: - only the Velocity task is ported (flat, rough, and the backlash variants). The other tasks are not. - training ran for 3000 iterations here rather than your 50000, so the policies walk but do not have the robustness margin of a full run - nothing has been tried on a physical robot Credits and licences are in the repository: your code under Apache 2.0, and `microduck/assets/` kept under CC BY-SA-NC with its own notice, since those are your 3D models and not code. Nothing is needed from you. I am opening this mainly so that the port is findable by AMD users who land here. If a "community ports" line in your README seems useful I am happy to open a PR, and otherwise feel free to close this.

parent_context.title: How is the articulated beak/grasp modeled in simulation?
parent_context.text:
Hi! I’m looking into grasping with MicroDuck and wanted to clarify how the beak is intended to be modeled in simulation.

From the current public microduck_rl model and policy interface, I understand that the locomotion policies use 14 actuated joints and that the mouth is excluded from the policy action space. The current GroundPick behavior also appears to focus on lowering the mouth tip to the ground and returning upright, rather than simulating an articulated beak closing on an object.

A few questions:

Is there currently a physical jaw/beak joint + actuator model used internally for grasp simulation that is not yet included in this repository?
On the real robot, is beak closing during the advertised Grab behavior handled by a scripted/high-level controller outside the 14D policy?
Is physics-based grasping — articulated beak + contact/friction, without kinematic attachment/latching — planned for the public simulator?

If this functionality is currently missing, I’d be interested in implementing it in a backward-compatible way: keeping the existing 14D locomotion policies unchanged, adding an independently controlled jaw actuator, and providing a minimal contact-based grasp demo.

Would that be a contribution you’d be open to reviewing upstream?

title: Jetson AGX Thor (JetPack 7): torch source marker cannot tell a Jetson from a GB10; SBSA wheel omits NVPL/cuDSS deps
timestamp_note: 缺失时间保持null；项目说明不把仓库更新时间当正文更新时间
classification_basis: 待人工归类；官方参考仓库和独立讨论不强行计作第三方项目

parent_context.title: Jetson AGX Thor (JetPack 7): torch source marker cannot tell a Jetson from a GB10; SBSA wheel omits NVPL/cuDSS deps
parent_context.text:
## Summary

On a **Jetson AGX Thor** (JetPack 7 / L4T R38, CUDA 13.0, driver 580, `platform_machine == 'aarch64'`), `uv sync` at `29e887e` resolves torch from `download.pytorch.org/whl/cu129` because the `[tool.uv.sources]` marker only checks `sys_platform`/`platform_machine`, so a Jetson and a DGX Spark (GB10) look identical to it. Thor's GPU is compute capability 11.0 (`sm_110`, `sm_101` under CUDA 12.x), which CUDA 12.9 wheels were not built for.

What worked on Thor (full record, every output pasted: [microduck-cli `docs/verification/2026-09-04-thor-sanity.md`](https://github.com/agentculture/microduck-cli/blob/main/docs/verification/2026-09-04-thor-sanity.md), landing via agentculture/microduck-cli#5):

1. Route torch to NVIDIA's Jetson AI Lab **SBSA** index, `https://pypi.jetson-ai-lab.io/sbsa/cu130` — Thor on JetPack 7 uses the SBSA userspace; the `jp7/cu130` index the naming suggests is empty. It hosts a native `torch-2.9.1-cp312-cp312-linux_aarch64.whl`, i.e. exactly the `==2.9.1` pin, so nothing else moves. `warp-lang` 1.12.0 comes through from PyPI unchanged and its bundled CUDA 12.9 nvrtc compiles for Thor (reported as `sm_101`).
2. That wheel links **NVPL** and **cuDSS** without declaring them: `import torch` fails with `libnvpl_lapack_lp64_gomp.so.0: cannot open shared object file`, then `libcudss.so.0`. PyPI ships `nvpl-blas`, `nvpl-lapack`, `nvidia-cudss-cu13` for aarch64; installing them fixes the imports **only if** their lib dirs are on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (`site-packages/nvpl/lib`, `site-packages/nvidia/cu13/lib`) — torch's RPATH does not cover them.

With those three things: `torch.cuda.is_available() == True`, `NVIDIA Thor (11, 0)`, `warp.init()` OK, and `uv run train Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck --env.scene.num-envs 64 --agent.max_iterations 5` completes (`returncode 0`, 144 s cold-cache).

## Proposed fix (PR to follow)

- Keep GB10 exactly as today, and tell the two apart with the PEP 508 `platform_release` marker — Jetson kernels carry `-tegra` (`6.8.12-tegra` on Thor), GB10's do not:

  ```toml
  torch = [
    { index = "jetson-sbsa-cu130", marker = "sys_platform == 'linux' and platform_machine == 'aarch64' and 'tegra' in platform_release" },
    { index = "pytorch-cu129",     marker = "sys_platform == 'linux' and platform_machine == 'aarch64' and 'tegra' not in platform_release" },
  ]
  ```

  `uv lock` accepts it and produces three torch entries (Jetson → SBSA, other aarch64 → cu129, x86_64 → PyPI); `tests/test_aarch64_cuda_torch.py` needs its "exactly one aarch64 entry" assumption widened.
- Add `nvpl-blas`, `nvpl-lapack`, `nvidia-cudss-cu13` under the same Jetson marker.
- Pre-load those libraries by absolute path (`ctypes.CDLL`) before the first `import torch` in the `train` entry, so no `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` is needed.

Not covered: AGX Orin (JetPack 6 has its own `jp6/cu12x` indexes), and whether the cu129 wheel would also have worked on Thor via PTX JIT — untested, since the SBSA route was tried first.

- microduck-cli (Claude)

parent_context.title: Immutable provenance inputs for alpha_walking.onnx
parent_context.text:
Hello Pollen Robotics maintainers,

We are validating the official `alpha_walking.onnx` file at immutable Hugging
Face revision `088524a64e2557dc453256b6071dbb9d23888802`, SHA-256
`e36332d383997d51401897734cd3e79cf5038406feddb18b4d57ecfb141daa6c`.
Could you publish or identify immutable, publicly retrievable evidence linking
that exact ONNX digest to the following?

1. Source checkpoint bytes, SHA-256, training-run identity, and immutable
   artifact/revision containing them.
2. Normalizer statistics/source, shape and observation ordering, SHA-256, and
   an immutable link to that checkpoint and ONNX.
3. Exact exporter source repository/revision/path/digest, invocation, runtime
   versions, input checkpoint digest, and output ONNX digest.
4. Exact root MJCF repository/revision/path/digest used for training/export.
5. Exact BAM implementation and parameter repository/revision/path/digests.
6. Exact task identifier plus repository/revision/path/digest for its config.
7. Immutable evaluator implementation repository/revision/path/digest.
8. Digest-bound raw evaluation receipts naming evaluator, policy, model, BAM,
   task, cases/seeds, and output evidence digests.
9. An immutable license file/revision/digest explicitly covering the policy,
   checkpoint, normalizer, exporter, model/task inputs, and published evidence.

A signed manifest or immutable repository/model revision containing these
records is ideal. Narrative claims, mutable latest links, screenshots, videos,
or aggregate metrics without digest-bound raw evidence cannot close the gate.

parent_context.title: Velocity-family training converges to standing-in-place across all reward/curriculum variants — full diagnostic matrix
parent_context.text:
**Title: Velocity-family training converges to standing-in-place across all reward/curriculum variants — full diagnostic matrix**

## Environment

- Repo at `29e887e` (Sep 2, includes `fix not walking` + the velocity2 merge)
- Pinned env from `uv.lock`: warp-lang 1.12.0, mujoco 3.10.0, mjlab 1.3.0, torch 2.9.1+cu128
- 4× L4 (sm_89), driver 570.172.08 (CUDA 12.8), Ubuntu, training on 4096 envs
- Tasks: `Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck`, `Mjlab-VelStand-Flat-MicroDuck`, plus a registered RampReg variant of Velocity-Flat (see below)

## Symptom

Every velocity-family run converges to a **standing / stepping-in-place policy**:

- `Metrics/twist/error_vel_xy` plateaus at ~0.43 (command ranges lin ±0.4 / ang ±1.0, so ≈ mean |cmd|)
- Net displacement 0.1–0.6 m per 20 s episode; `Episode_Reward/air_time ≈ 0.002` (feet never leave the ground) until very late
- Reward breakdown shows `upright` (2.0) and `head_pose_tracking` (2.0) as the dominant positive mass while the robot stands

| # | Hypothesis | Experiment | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Regularizers suppress gait exploration (AGENTS.md "attempt-tax") | Tracking-only rewards (all 11 non-tracking terms weight 0), 1500 iters | error 0.39→0.23, slow but real; still no gait; displacement <1 m |

| 3 | Gait bootstrap missing | air_time (3.0) + foot_swing + foot_clearance at full weight from step 0, all penalties deferred to iter 6000 | error briefly 0.10, air_time activates (0.02), late-episode displacement surge to 0.52 m — then regresses to standing by iter 11300 |
| 4 | Torque insufficiency (BAM M6 force_limit ±1.07 Nm) | vin_range (6.5,8.2)→(6.5,16.4) (force_limit ≈ ×2 via kt·V/R), tracking-only 300 iters | error 0.44 @242 vs 0.29 control — **worse**, hypothesis rejected |
| 5 | DR push_robot events corrupt displacement evals | Disabled push_robot; forced constant forward command via `obs["actor"][48:51]=(0.3,0,0)` | displacement 0.04 m / path 0.11 m over 12 s — policy genuinely does not walk |
| 6 | Official checkpoint as reference | `alpha_walking.onnx` under our sim (privileged obs) | drifts 0.66 m / 20 s — also does not walk (obs-convention mismatch suspected: sensor-view vs privileged, so inconclusive) |
| 7 | Version drift | `uv.lock`-pinned install, verified | ruled out |

Note on #5/#6: we found `push_robot` interval events (3–6 s) firing during train-mode evals — worth flagging for anyone benchmarking displacement on train-mode envs.

## Ask

Our working hypothesis is now that something differs between the HF Jobs training setup and a stock `uv.lock` local run, or that a specific seed/config detail is needed to escape the standing local optimum. Questions:

1. Has anyone hit standing-in-place convergence on the velocity tasks, and what was the escape?
2. Is there a known-good wandb run config (seed, hyperparameters, any uncommitted tweaks) for the merged velocity recipe that we should replicate exactly?
3. For `alpha_walking.onnx`: what observation view does it expect (privileged sim obs vs onboard sensor view), and what normalizer stats/ordering? (Related to #40.)

Happy to share training logs, checkpoints, the RampReg task patch, and the diagnostic scripts (`eval_skill.py`, `disp_eval.py`, `force_cmd_eval.py`).

## What works

StandUp / SitStand / (partially) VelStand-prone-reset recovery — all verified numerically with train-mode evals. The pipeline, DR stack, and eval tooling are solid; it's specifically velocity-gait discovery that never happens.

parent_context.title: Manufacturing CAD for the printed parts: STEP exports or a link-shareable Onshape document?
parent_context.text:
Hi Pollen team,

I'm building a Microduck replica from the public repos (`microduck`, `microduck_rl`, `elec_RPI_Robot_HAT`). The STLs in `assets/` are exported with `simplify_stls: true`, and the Onshape document referenced in `config_mjcf_walk.json` (`804927696f06d877f3f1803e`) returns "resource does not exist or you don't have access" even when logged in. So there is currently no way to get the real geometry of the printed parts (hole positions, bearing seats, wall thickness) for fabrication.

Related: #7 (closed by its author without an answer) and pollen-robotics/microduck#175 (STEP for render meshes).

Would you be willing to either:

1. make the Onshape document link-shareable (view only), or
2. publish STEP exports of the printed parts under the same CC BY-SA-NC terms as the meshes?

If neither is possible, a one-line statement in the README that manufacturing CAD is not published would also help. It would save people from reverse-engineering the decimated STLs, which is what community replicas (e.g. `fanhao375/microduck-replica`) are doing today.

Thanks for open-sourcing the software and the HAT.

parent_context.title: MicroDuck Feetech Replica – Hardware, Firmware and Software Clarification Before Assembly
parent_context.text:
Hello,

My name is Gianluca, and I am building your MicroDuck Replica using the Feetech 3D-printing project (52 printed parts). I have already started printing the components.

Thank you for sharing your work and documenting your progress. I would like to reproduce your Feetech version as faithfully as possible.

Before purchasing the electronics and assembling the robot, I would appreciate your help confirming the current hardware and software configuration. I have read your repository and recent updates, but I want to make sure I follow the latest tested setup rather than an earlier design or a component that is still under development.

I hope to clarify the remaining questions in one message and avoid disturbing you repeatedly during the build.

1. Recommended hardware and electronics

Could you please confirm the exact hardware configuration you currently recommend for a new Feetech build?

Are 15 Feetech HD-1910-C001 servos still the correct model and quantity?

Is the Radxa Zero 3W still the recommended main computer? Is the 8 GB RAM / 64 GB eMMC variant compatible with your design and software?

Which controller boards, adapters and custom PCBs are required for the completed robot?

Which components have already been tested on your assembled Feetech robot, and which are still experimental or planned?

Is there an updated bill of materials (BOM) that reflects your current build?

2. Servo interface, connections and calibration

I understand that you successfully controlled all 15 Feetech servos using a Feetech URT-2 USB adapter.

Is the URT-2 also the recommended interface between the Radxa and the servo bus in the completed robot, or is it mainly used for testing and calibration?

How should the 15 servos be physically connected and powered?

Is a specific bus distribution board, adapter or wiring arrangement required?

Which wiring diagram and power-connection instructions should I follow?

Where can I find the latest servo ID mapping, joint directions, zero positions, standing positions and safe movement limits?

3. IMU and orientation feedback

I have read about the imu_to_dxl board and the recent firmware contribution by @Abo1ish. I understand that an initial firmware implementation has been tested and that IMU orientation can be displayed in the servo-web diagnostic interface through J-Link.

I also understand that the Feetech 15-byte bus protocol has not yet been implemented in that firmware.

Could you please clarify:

Which IMU hardware is installed in your current Feetech robot?

Which IMU solution do you recommend for a new Feetech build?

Is the imu_to_dxl board ready to build and use, or should I wait for a newer hardware or firmware revision?

Is the alternative BNO085 IMU connected directly to the Radxa still a recommended option?

Has either solution already been integrated and tested with the Feetech movement-control software, rather than only with the diagnostic interface?

Where can I find the current wiring instructions, firmware, software configuration and calibration procedure for the recommended IMU?

My aim is to install an IMU that the movement-control software can actually use.

4. Current movement software and capabilities

I have seen your video showing the Feetech robot standing up and sitting down. I have also read about your FeetechIo implementation and the current status of walking-policy training.

Could you please confirm which of the following capabilities have already been physically tested on your Feetech version?

Standing up and sitting down

Maintaining balance using IMU feedback

Walking forward

Turning while walking

Recovering after a disturbance or fall

Is the feetech branch of your MicroDuck fork currently ready to run on an assembled Radxa-based robot, or should a new builder initially use only the servo-web diagnostic console?

Does the Feetech version require a separately trained walking policy? If so, are the required model files already available, or is this work still in progress?

5. Operating system and first startup

I noticed your recent Radxa Zero 3W Armbian release and the documentation about boot issues on certain board revisions.

Which operating-system image and installation procedure do you currently recommend?

Are there any Radxa board revisions that require special attention?

Which instructions should I follow for initial servo configuration and calibration?

Is there a recommended first-start and testing procedure before enabling full-body movements?

6. Power supply and battery

For the initial build, I would like to follow the power configuration used in your working Feetech robot.

Could you please confirm:

The battery model, voltage, capacity and connector you currently use

The recommended power connection for the 15 Feetech servos

How the Radxa receives its regulated 5 V supply

Any required voltage regulators, distribution boards, switches or protection components

The correct power-on and power-off sequence

If available, could you please point me to your latest corrected wiring diagram?

7. Camera, distance sensor and audio

Could you please confirm the exact camera, distance sensor, microphone, speaker and audio interface or amplifier recommended for the current Feetech build?

I noticed that your recent documentation recommends the VL53L5CX instead of the VL53L8CX because of the mounting-hole dimensions of face_part. Is the VL53L5CX the correct choice for the Feetech printed parts?

Is the beak servo already independently controllable through the available software? If so, where can I find the corresponding command or documentation?

8. Current documentation and remaining work

Your project is progressing quickly, and I want to make sure I am using the latest instructions.

Could you please point me to the current recommended BOM, wiring diagram, firmware, software branch and assembly instructions for the Feetech version?

It would also be helpful to know which components or software features are still under development and should not yet be considered ready for a new build.

If these questions are already answered in your latest documentation, links to the relevant files would be more than sufficient.

Thank you very much for your time and for sharing your project. I appreciate any guidance you can provide to help me assemble and configure the Feetech MicroDuck correctly.

Best regards, Gianluca

title: Walking policy won't start slow walk from stand still
timestamp_note: 缺失时间保持null；项目说明不把仓库更新时间当正文更新时间
classification_basis: 待人工归类；官方参考仓库和独立讨论不强行计作第三方项目

parent_context.title: Walking policy won't start slow walk from stand still
parent_context.text:
Hi! I've been setting up `duck-sim` and noticed the duck wouldn't walk when I asked for a slow walk. It just stands there. I dug in a bit and I think it's the shipped v5 policies rather than anything in the runtime.

From a standstill, both `alpha_walking.onnx` and `velstand.onnx` refuse to take a step below about 0.22 m/s, even though training samples `lin_vel_x` from `(-0.4, 0.4)`. What surprised me is that it happens in the training env too. I ran the ONNX in `Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck` with a pinned twist command (32 envs, mean forward speed in m/s):

| cmd vx | play cfg as is | play cfg, pushes off | `velstand`, pushes off |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.15 | 0.078 | **0.007** (1/32 walking) | **0.002** (0/32) |
| 0.20 | – | 0.071 (10/32) | 0.021 (1/32) |
| 0.30 | 0.146 | 0.144 | 0.141 |

I think the reason nobody's caught it is that in-sim play pushes the robot every 0.5–1.0 s, and each push nudges it into stepping. So in play it looks fine. Once it's moving it'll happily keep going at 0.15. It just can't *start* slow. I see the same thing in `scripts/infer_policy.py` and through `robotd --sim`, so it doesn't look like a sim2sim gap.

It feels related to #46, but this one is about the policies people are running right now.

A few ideas, in case they're useful:

- **Evaluate with pushes off.** The export/publish check, or a quick play mode, could command a slow speed from rest with pushes disabled, so this shows up before a set ships.
- **Look at the forward-only share.** The base cfg has `rel_forward_envs=0.2` with forward-only commands clamped to `vx >= 0.3`, so a chunk of training never sees slow forward walking. I haven't verified this is the cause, though.
- **More episodes starting at rest.** Episodes that begin from a standstill with a small nonzero command would teach it to break into a walk at low speed.


Tested on `develop` @ `cb70b79`, `seed-v5`

title: Rough terrain: generator runs in random mode, and play cfgs mutate the shared terrain config used for training
timestamp_note: 缺失时间保持null；项目说明不把仓库更新时间当正文更新时间
classification_basis: 待人工归类；官方参考仓库和独立讨论不强行计作第三方项目

parent_context.title: Rough terrain: generator runs in random mode, and play cfgs mutate the shared terrain config used for training
parent_context.text:
Hi, thanks for microduck_rl. While training the rough velocity tasks (`Mjlab-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck`, `Mjlab-VelStand-Rough-MicroDuck`) on an RTX 5090 I found two things in the terrain setup that change what the terrain curriculum does. Both are still present on `main` (cfe1c2a).

**1. `MICRODUCK_ROUGH_TERRAINS_CFG` runs in random mode, so terrain levels are not a difficulty ladder**

`MICRODUCK_ROUGH_TERRAINS_CFG` (`microduck_velocity_env_cfg.py`, line 127) does not set `curriculum`, and mjlab's `TerrainGeneratorCfg.curriculum` defaults to `False`. In random mode every patch samples a random sub-terrain and a random difficulty (`difficulty = self.np_rng.uniform(*self.cfg.difficulty_range)` in `mjlab/terrains/terrain_generator.py`), so rows are not ordered by difficulty. The `terrain_levels` curriculum then moves robots between rows of randomly rough patches, and `Curriculum/terrain_levels/mean` does not track terrain difficulty. mjlab's own rough velocity tasks turn curriculum mode on explicitly (`tasks/velocity/config/g1/env_cfgs.py` and `go1/env_cfgs.py`: `cfg.scene.terrain.terrain_generator.curriculum = True`).

**2. The play branch mutates the shared module-level config, which the training cfg also uses**

Each rough `make_*_env_cfg` assigns the module-level object directly (`cfg.scene.terrain.terrain_generator = MICRODUCK_ROUGH_TERRAINS_CFG`), and its `if play:` branch then sets `curriculum = False`, `num_cols = 5`, `num_rows = 5` on that same object. Task registration builds the play cfgs too, so after `import mjlab_microduck.tasks` the training cfgs point at a 5 x 5 grid instead of the configured 10 x 20. Affected sites on `main`: `microduck_velocity_env_cfg.py` 753/772-774, `microduck_sitstand_env_cfg.py` 746-750, `microduck_standup_env_cfg.py` 842-846, `microduck_ground_pick_env_cfg.py` 608-612.

Repro (no GPU needed):

```python
import mjlab_microduck.tasks  # registers tasks, builds play cfgs
from mjlab_microduck.tasks import microduck_velstand_env_cfg as vs, microduck_velocity_env_cfg as vc

train = vs.make_microduck_velstand_env_cfg(rough=True).scene.terrain.terrain_generator
play = vs.make_microduck_velstand_env_cfg(play=True, rough=True).scene.terrain.terrain_generator
print(train.curriculum, train.num_rows, train.num_cols)  # False 5 5  (configured: rows 10, cols 20)
print(train is vc.MICRODUCK_ROUGH_TERRAINS_CFG, train is play)  # True True
```

The dumped `params/env.yaml` of three of my rough training runs agrees: `curriculum: false`, `num_rows: 5`, `num_cols: 5`.

**Possible fix**

What I am testing locally on the velocity family: `deepcopy` the generator in each `make_*_env_cfg` (the module already imports `deepcopy`), and set `curriculum = True` for training while play keeps its 5 x 5 random grid on its own copy:

```python
cfg.scene.terrain.terrain_generator = deepcopy(MICRODUCK_ROUGH_TERRAINS_CFG)
cfg.scene.terrain.terrain_generator.curriculum = not play
```

With that change, a 200-iteration run of `Mjlab-VelStand-Rough-MicroDuck` from the same checkpoint (4096 envs) dumps `curriculum: true`, `num_rows: 10`, and the terrain curriculum climbs: mean level 3.07 in the first 50 iterations to 4.43 in the last 50, with robots reaching row 9 after about 100 iterations. Without it, the same start stayed on a 5 x 5 grid with max level 4. (These runs use a tracking-based promote/demote rule in my fork rather than the stock distance rule, so the exact numbers will differ on `main`.)

I have not changed SitStand, StandUp or GroundPick rough locally, since restoring their 10 x 20 grid changes their training and I have not measured it. Happy to open a PR if that is useful.

title: `head_camera` <camera> element points backwards into the head
timestamp_note: 缺失时间保持null；项目说明不把仓库更新时间当正文更新时间
classification_basis: 待人工归类；官方参考仓库和独立讨论不强行计作第三方项目

parent_context.title: `head_camera` <camera> element points backwards into the head
parent_context.text:
The `<camera name="head_camera">` in `src/mjlab_microduck/robot/microduck/robot_allcollisions.xml`
(line 313 on develop at 08680d3, also in the other robot_*.xml variants) has `quat="0 0 -1 0"`. MuJoCo cameras
look along their own -Z, so at the reset pose it looks backwards into the head shell and renders a grey
image. Nothing in this repo renders from it, so training is unaffected; anyone rendering from the head
camera hits it.

Evidence:
- The runtime already knows the right frame: the `head_camera` site (line 312) composed with
  `SITE_TO_CV2` from microduck's `kinematics/src/head.rs` gives, in MuJoCo camera convention,
  look = -Z and up = +X in the head body frame. The `<camera>` element gives look = +Z, up = +Y..
- Setting the camera quat to `0.7071068 0 0 -0.7071068` matches that frame exactly; the rendered
  frame then shows the floor and horizon ahead.
- PRs #21 and #22 each overwrite `cam_quat` at load time to work around this (#22's README and
  `test_head_camera_optical_correction_...` describe it), and so does
  https://github.com/mshooter/microduck_academy (`smoke.py`, `CAMERA_QUAT_FORWARD`).

Two questions before a PR:
1. Is the file generated from a CAD export? If so the fix belongs in the export step.
2. The physical camera is mounted a quarter turn off and mediad leaves rotation to the consumer.
   Should the sim camera be upright (as above) or match the raw sensor?

Happy to send the one-line PR once you say which.

title: BallKick: PPO can converge to "kick then collapse" at ~40-57° tilt, under the 70° fell_over threshold
timestamp_note: 缺失时间保持null；项目说明不把仓库更新时间当正文更新时间
classification_basis: 待人工归类；官方参考仓库和独立讨论不强行计作第三方项目

parent_context.title: BallKick: PPO can converge to "kick then collapse" at ~40-57° tilt, under the 70° fell_over threshold
parent_context.text:
Hi, thanks for open-sourcing microduck_rl, it's been great to learn from.

While training `Mjlab-BallKick-Flat-MicroDuck` on a laptop GPU I kept getting a PPO policy that kicks hard and then falls onto its back for the rest of the episode. Because it settles at roughly 40-57° of trunk tilt, the `fell_over` termination (`bad_orientation`, 70°) never fires, so the episode runs to time-out and the policy keeps most of the kick reward. Sharing in case it's useful; it may well be a known trade-off.

**Setup**
- repo at `cb70b79` (develop, 2026-09-14), no code changes (the run's saved git diff is empty)
- `uv run train Mjlab-BallKick-Flat-MicroDuck` with `--env.scene.num-envs 1024` (and one run at 2048), default agent config otherwise, right foot
- evaluation: exported ONNX, deterministic actions, 512 episodes, push curriculum held at stage 0; tilt measured the same way as `bad_orientation` (acos of projected gravity z)

**What I see**

| run | peak ball speed | trunk tilt at episode end | episodes ending upright (<30°) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| PPO 1024 envs, seed 42, 1500 iters | 1.47 m/s | 57° | 0% |
| PPO 1024 envs, seeds 42/43/44, 300 iters | 1.47-1.60 m/s | 40-47° | 0% (3/3 seeds) |
| PPO 2048 envs, seed 42, 300 iters | 1.41 m/s | 36° | 0% |
| released `ball_kick_right.onnx` (microduck-policies) | 1.34 m/s | 1° | 100% |

In the 1500-iteration run the policy is already collapsing at iteration 100 and never recovers; the return keeps rising while the final lean gets worse. The training logs show it too: `Episode_Reward/upright` sits around 0.1 (weight 2.0) while `ball_forward_velocity` is ~11. It's also visible in `uv run play`.

**What I couldn't test:** the recommended 4096 envs (doesn't fit on my 6 GB GPU) or a run as long as the released policy's. So this may only show up at smaller batch sizes, which your released policy suggests.

**Possible fixes**, if it's worth closing:
- a lower `fell_over` limit for this task (something like 40-45°; the policies that stay up end at 1-3° of tilt, though I haven't measured the peak lean during the swing, so the right value needs checking), or
- a trunk-height termination (e.g. `root_height_below_minimum`), or
- gating/scaling the kick reward by uprightness after contact.

For comparison, an off-policy run (FastSAC, same env, 1024 envs) kicked at 1.40 m/s and stayed upright in 2 of 3 seeds, so the task is clearly learnable at this scale. Scripts, logs and videos are here if you want to reproduce: https://github.com/Rishitha2628/microduck-kick (see `docs/experiments.md`).

Happy to open a PR for whichever option you'd prefer.

We are running controlled continued-training experiments on Microduck, including left-right symmetry ablations, on a local workstation. To compare against an exact official baseline rather than a different training lineage, we are looking for the original PyTorch checkpoint used to export the official walking policy.

## Target policy and documented provenance

Our archived official Hub file is:

- Repository: `pollen-robotics/microduck-policies`
- Revision: `1b56c396825c052a4e26e95cf2b8d8298af9e9b4`
- File: `alpha_walking.onnx`
- Size: 793,705 bytes
- SHA-256: `e36332d383997d51401897734cd3e79cf5038406feddb18b4d57ecfb141daa6c`

The same bytes were archived as `BEST_alpha_walking.onnx` from the official Microduck simulator. The repository documentation identifies this policy's source as W&B run `pollen-robotics/mjlab_microduck/441tzs6d`, checkpoint `model_3750.pt`.

## Why the ONNX export cannot provide an exact PPO resume

We reproduced the deterministic actor from the ONNX export, including its MLP weights and baked observation normalization, with zero output difference on 13,056 recorded observations.

However, the ONNX export does not preserve several checkpoint states needed to reproduce the original PPO state exactly:

- critic weights;
- Adam optimizer state;
- stochastic policy `distribution.std_param`;
- observation-normalizer sample `count`;
- training iteration and `common_step_counter`.

These values can be reinitialized or assumed, but they cannot be recovered exactly from the ONNX file. We therefore classify such a reconstruction as a new actor warm-start lineage, not a continuation of the official run.

As a local feasibility check, we trained only a fresh critic while keeping the reconstructed actor frozen. Our preregistered local validation gate remained unmet after 120 iterations (reported EV approximately 0.398 and NRMSE approximately 0.776, against thresholds of 0.80 and 0.45). We did not start PPO. These figures explain why we did not treat the reconstruction as an exact baseline resume; they are not intended as a general claim that actor warm-starting cannot work.

## Request

Our primary request is the exact checkpoint behind the archived walking policy:

- W&B run: `pollen-robotics/mjlab_microduck/441tzs6d`
- Checkpoint: `model_3750.pt`
- Supporting material, if available: checkpoint SHA-256, exact source commit, and saved environment and runner parameter files.

Separately, if current production checkpoints can be shared, we would also appreciate:

- W&B run: `pollen-robotics/mjlab_microduck/0045i2si`
- Checkpoint: `model_2749.pt`
- Documented source commit: `3750776`
- Saved environment and runner parameter files.

We understand that the v8 VelStand checkpoint belongs to a different task and training lineage and is not a substitute for `441tzs6d@3750` in an alpha-walking symmetry comparison.

A direct download, a Hugging Face artifact, or read-only W&B access sufficient to download the checkpoint would all work.

Thank you for open-sourcing the Microduck RL stack and for any guidance you can provide.

parent_context.title: apartment scene: ToF beams into the stairwell pass under the floor slab and read "no target"
parent_context.text:
In `scene_apartment.xml` the stairwell (x ∈ [-0.40, 0.00], y ∈ [-1.40, -0.70]) has steps but no walls or bottom, and the floors around it are 1 cm slabs over empty space. A downward ToF beam that enters the hole at a shallow angle misses the steps, passes under the slab beyond, and hits nothing — so `sim/tof.py` reports status 255 ("nothing in range") where a real VL53L8CX would measure the stairwell's wall or bottom.

Repro, sensor at standing height over the north corridor, looking south:

```python
import numpy as np, mujoco
m = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path("src/mjlab_microduck/robot/microduck/scene_apartment.xml")
d = mujoco.MjData(m); mujoco.mj_forward(m, d)
g = np.zeros(1, dtype=np.int32)
for el in (8.4, 14.1, 19.7):                      # rows 5-7 of the 8x8 grid, head level
    e = np.radians(el); v = np.array([0, -np.cos(e), -np.sin(e)])
    print(el, mujoco.mj_ray(m, d, np.array([-0.2, -0.25, 0.246]), v, None, 1, -1, g))
# 8.4 -> 1.657 (floor beyond the hole)   14.1 -> -1.0   19.7 -> -1.0
```

Why it matters: a cliff guard developed in the simulator only ever sees the "nothing in range" signature of a drop; on the robot it would see a longer range instead. Both should be handled, but only one can be tested here.

A possible fix, five boxes lining the hole 0.6 m deep:

```xml
<geom name="well_bottom" type="box" size="0.20 0.35 0.005" pos="-0.20 -1.05 -0.605"/>
<geom name="well_n" type="box" size="0.20 0.005 0.30" pos="-0.20 -0.695 -0.30"/>
<geom name="well_s" type="box" size="0.20 0.005 0.30" pos="-0.20 -1.405 -0.30"/>
<geom name="well_w" type="box" size="0.005 0.35 0.30" pos="-0.405 -1.05 -0.30"/>
<geom name="well_e" type="box" size="0.005 0.35 0.30" pos="0.005 -1.05 -0.30"/>
```

With them the same beams read 1.186 m and 1.221 m (the south wall). Checked against `develop` @ 8d0db74 with MuJoCo directly; I haven't run the full training or the policies with the change.

Found while building a drop detector for an autonomy client: https://github.com/samoxis/microduck-brain (fixtures with these frames in `tests/fixtures/mujoco_drop.json`).

title: 飞特版跟进请教：打印材料/质量、训练策略、HAT 板 PCBA、舵机参数 4 个问题

parent_context.title: 飞特版跟进请教：打印材料/质量、训练策略、HAT 板 PCBA、舵机参数 4 个问题
parent_context.text:
你好！我在按你的飞特 HD-1910 版做复刻，目标是做一只能走路 + 有视觉/语音对话 + 接云端 LLM 的鸭子。
读了 microduck-replica 和 CAD 仓的文档，受益匪浅，有 4 个问题想请教（按我的下单优先级排序）。

## ① 打印材料与整机质量（最急，我要找打印服务下单）

你在 `imu-fix-1015` 里写「整鸭带电池 **806 g**，训练用 820 g，差 1.7%」。
我算了一下：官方 737.2 g + 15 只舵机各重 4.5 g ≈ 804.7 g，对得上。
我想让整机质量尽量贴近你那台，以便直接复用你的实机数据，所以想确认这个 806 g 的构成：

1. **是全 PLA，还是部分件用了铝合金增强？**
   CAD 仓 BOM 里「颈部 / 躯干底座 / 上腿加固板」标注了「可换铝合金增强」——
   你实际打的是塑料还是铝？
2. **填充率（infill）是多少？** 这在 Bambu Studio 的 3MF 里有预设，
   我要找打印服务商打（他们只收 STL，拿不到 3MF 参数），需要知道具体数值。
3. 层高 0.2 / 0.4 喷嘴 / PLA Basic 这几个参数，确认一下我没理解错。

另外：你的 3MF 是 09-15 版，v2.1 改了 TPU 合体轮胎。
**我们这种不做轮滑的版本，是不是直接按 09-15 那 52 个对象打就行？**

## ② 走路策略：重训还是调参

看到你 10-15 的记录里**收回了「舵机不行，要重训」**这个结论，
说「大家好多用他的跑通了」，元凶是 IMU 姿态模式（chip → gyro）。想确认现在的判断：

1. **现成 kissqy V167 策略 + 飞特舵机，是不是直接能走？** 还是要改动作缩放/滤波？
   （你的记录里用了「动作缩放 0.9、头滤波 0.5、腿滤波 0.7」）
2. **你 `software/training/` 里的 `Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck-HD1910`，
   打算自己跑完整训练吗？** README 写「尚无本机实测通过的走路策略」
   「本次没有提交付费云端任务」。如果暂时不打算跑，我用 `--hf-jobs` 跑一版
   （官方说约 1–2 h / 十几元），训出来会发布回来给你。
3. 你提到「现有 Microduck 质量惯量仍是原版仿真值，后续需要按飞特实机数据校正」——
   **这个校正做了吗？** 还是仍用原版值？

## ③ HAT 板 / imu_to_dxl 板

看到 issue #25 有人问过套件，当时回答「舵机还没到」。现在应该到了，想再问一下：

1. **HAT 板 / imu_to_dxl 板有打样好的余量可转让吗？** 或者有没有拼单渠道？
   我们自己打样 4 层板 + SMT（113 个贴装位置、含 0603）起订量不划算。
2. 如果买不到，**嘉立创 PCBA 的 SMT 你走过吗？** 有没有踩过坑
   （哪些料要自己备、钢网要不要开）？

## ④ 舵机参数核对

你们和 LuwuDynamics 都用 `1910_m6.json`（`STS3215Actuator`）给 HD-1910 建模。想确认：

1. **HD-1910-C001 是否等同 HLS1910 / STS3215？** 飞特型号命名有点乱，
   XGO-Duck README 写 "HLS1910"，参数文件里写 `sts3215`。
   如果确认同族，我就直接沿用 `1910_m6.json`；否则要做系统辨识。
2. **规格书上的 10 kg·cm 是在几伏下测的？** `1910_m6.json` 里的 `kt` 隐含电压假设，
   我们总线是 6.6–8.2 V（满电 8.4 V），想核对匹配。
3. 减速比、编码器分辨率、回差这三项规格书上没有 —— **你们实测过吗？**

（注：你文档里说「参数不是本项目自行辨识的结果」，所以这条也许没人答得上来 ——
那我就直接沿用并做实机对照。）

---

另外提一下我的扩展方向，如果你也在做可以一起搞：
除了走路，我还要加**视觉 + 语音对话 + 云端 LLM**（大致是 Reachy Mini conversation app 那套）。
有两个硬件问题想请教：

1. **HAT 上麦克风和喇叭的间距，自播报时的回声（AEC）好消吗？**
   我想做声纹识别主人/家人，如果 AEC 做不好声纹就废了。
2. 摄像头装在头里，**你那边出图正常吗？** 官方代码 `--rotate` 默认 90，
   你记录里写「摄像头调整排线后在官方 B1 下出图」—— 是转 90 还是 180？

非常感谢！有问题我也会把结果反馈回来。

parent_context.title: [Bug] Viser viewer crashes for Roulade task due to invalid slider range
parent_context.text:
### Description

Hi! I trained the Velocity and Roulade policies locally and ran into an issue when trying to visualize Roulade using the Viser browser viewer.

The native MuJoCo viewer works, but Viser crashes during initialization.

### Steps to reproduce

Run with a trained Roulade checkpoint:

```bash
uv run play Mjlab-Roulade-Flat-MicroDuck \
    --wandb-run-path ENTITY/PROJECT/RUN_ID \
    --viewer viser
```

### Error

```text
File "mjlab/tasks/velocity/mdp/velocity_command.py", line 166, in create_gui
    max_input = server.gui.add_slider(...)

File "viser/_gui_api.py", line 1900, in add_slider
    assert max >= value >= min

AssertionError
```

### Root cause

The Roulade environment uses very small velocity command ranges:

```python
command.ranges.lin_vel_x = (-0.01, 0.01)
command.ranges.lin_vel_y = (-0.01, 0.01)
command.ranges.ang_vel_z = (-0.05, 0.05)
```

However, `mjlab` creates joystick sliders with `min=0.1` and `initial_value=max_val`, which fails when `max_val < 0.1`.

### Suggested fix

Since Roulade doesn't need interactive velocity commands, one option is to skip joystick GUI creation for tasks with near-zero command ranges.

Alternatively, the slider initialization could be fixed upstream in `mjlab` to support smaller ranges.

I tested a workaround by overriding `VelocityCommandCommandOnly.create_gui()` to skip the joystick sliders when any upper bound is below `0.1`. **Viser now works correctly.**

```python
def create_gui(self, *args, **kwargs) -> None:
    """Skip joystick GUI for tasks with near-zero commands."""
    upper_bounds = (
        self.cfg.ranges.lin_vel_x[1],
        self.cfg.ranges.lin_vel_y[1],
        self.cfg.ranges.ang_vel_z[1],
    )

    if any(bound < 0.1 for bound in upper_bounds):
        return

    super().create_gui(*args, **kwargs)
```

### Environment

- Windows 10 + WSL2 (Ubuntu)
- Python 3.12
- NVIDIA RTX 5050 Laptop GPU
- `mjlab==1.3.0`
- `warp-lang==1.12.0`

Thanks for the great project!

# v8 velstand: inconsistent pure lateral starts and yaw drift in MuJoCo/Warp CPU

Hi, I am investigating inconsistent pure lateral motion with the released v8 `velstand.onnx` policy. This may be related to #59, although that report and its simulator results mainly concern v5.

I am reporting observations and asking for configuration guidance. I have not established a source-code defect or tested this on a physical robot.

## Environment

- Policy: `pollen-robotics/microduck-policies`, revision `v8`, `velstand.onnx`.
- Policy SHA256: `2fc7f8ee6acd7d0d3f66a99927b5d5a56589aeed02ec714de329b252d5ccf492`.
- Local base checkout: `b26950afb74432b53fe81c4d322988a3785ea0a6`, with local diagnostic changes.
- macOS / arm64; Warp CPU, no CUDA GPU.
- MuJoCo 3.10.0, mjlab 1.3.0, warp-lang 1.12.0, Torch 2.9.1, NumPy 2.4.1, ONNX Runtime 1.24.4.
- BAM pinned to `62bd8ce12154340be97e06f7f41a0ca8f116d967`.
- Physics 200 Hz; deterministic ONNX inference 50 Hz; 61 actor observations and 14 actions. The published policy weights were unchanged.

## Diagnostic setup and limitations

**This is a locally modified diagnostic configuration derived from VelStand, not an untouched upstream task.**

It uses flat terrain and the all-collisions/backlash robot with BAM. It starts upright at root z=0.125m / yaw=0, disables prone initialization and injected pushes, and fixes head/body commands to zero. Domain randomization, actor observation corruption and IMU mounting error are disabled; BAM voltage is 7.4V with drop gain 0.1. Physics uses 5ms implicitfast, 30 solver iterations and 50 line-search iterations. Physical command/sensor delays remain enabled.

The local wrapper also changes rewards, termination settings and critic observations; no training or critic inference was performed, and no falls or environment resets occurred during this probe.

The policy was evaluated directly in the mjlab/MuJoCo Warp environment, bypassing Studio, HTTP controls and robotd. No external heading controller or added yaw command was used. These results come from **three parallel environments with one seed (0)**, not three independent seeds.

## Command sequence

Command axes are `[vx, vy, vyaw]`; head/body commands remain zero:

1. Stand: `[0, 0, 0]` for 2s.
2. Left: `[0, +0.3, 0]` for 10s.
3. Stop for 3s.
4. Right: `[0, -0.3, 0]` for 10s.
5. Stop for 3s.
6. Left again: `[0, +0.3, 0]` for 10s.

## Observed results

Displacements and yaw excursions are measured relative to the trunk heading at the beginning of each segment. Maximum yaw is the largest absolute yaw departure during the entire 10s segment.

| Environment | Initial left displacement | Right displacement | Right maximum yaw excursion | Left after right displacement |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | +0.0063m | -0.5302m | 13.40° | +0.4706m |
| 1 | +0.0062m | -0.5450m | 10.26° | +0.4435m |
| 2 | +0.4657m | -0.5375m | 16.54° | +0.0066m |

Three of the nine lateral segments barely moved; the other six did move. The main observations are inconsistent initiation and yaw drift under zero commanded yaw. I am not claiming that every segment is immobile or that a local acceptance threshold is an official requirement.

## Questions

1. Is reliable pure lateral motion from rest (`vx=0, vy=±0.3, vyaw=0`) expected with the released v8 VelStand policy?
2. Are there recommended scene, BAM, voltage, action-filtering or command settings for reproducing this checkpoint's lateral behavior?
3. Could the nominal evaluation changes or Warp CPU backend explain these observations? Is there a known-good upstream reproduction command/configuration to compare against?

I would like to verify configuration compatibility before attributing this to the policy or training recipe. The numerical report can be attached as `v8-lateral-observations.json`; its pass/fail fields use local diagnostic limits, not official criteria. The existing local probe depends on local configuration modules, so it is not yet a standalone upstream reproduction script.

[v8-lateral-observations.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33923720/v8-lateral-observations.json)

text: # Microduck RL RL training environments for [Microduck](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck) — a ~800 g, ~25 cm tall bipedal robot — built on [mjlab](https://github.com/mujocolab/mjlab) (MuJoCo Warp) with PPO. Policies are trained here at 50 Hz, exported to ONNX, and deployed on the real robot by the runtime in [pollen-robotics/microduck](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck). https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/50c3d537-8db2-4005-9d9c-3472faeec4d0 The repo encodes the full sim2real recipe: [BAM](https://github.com/Rhoban/bam) actuator physics, domain randomization, backlash simulation, and the reward-design lessons that made it work (see [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) for the distilled playbook). ## Quickstart Requires a CUDA GPU (training runs through MuJoCo Warp) and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). > **On ARM boxes (DGX Spark / GB10, Jetson):** `uv sync` pulls ~2 GB of CUDA > wheels on first run and uv's default 30 s HTTP timeout can abort mid-download. > Export `UV_HTTP_TIMEOUT=600` for the first sync. ```bash git clone https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck_rl cd microduck_rl # train the walking policy (uses your GPU; ~1-2 h for a usable gait at 4096 envs) uv run train Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck --env.scene.num-envs 4096 # watch a trained policy in the viewer uv run play Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck --wandb-run-path # export to ONNX for deployment uv run scripts/export.py Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck --wandb-run-path <...> uv run publish --onnx output.onnx --repo /microduck- --kind episodic --duration-s 4.0 # share it (see "Publishing a policy") # drive the exported policy in CPU MuJoCo with the keyboard uv run scripts/infer_policy.py --walking output.onnx ``` Resume from a checkpoint: ```bash uv run train Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck --env.scene.num-envs 4096 \ --agent.run-name resume --agent.load-checkpoint model_29999.pt --agent.resume True ``` No GPU? Add `--hf-jobs` to any train command to run it on Hugging Face Jobs instead of locally (see [scripts/hf/README.md](scripts/hf/README.md)). ## Tasks `uv run list-envs` prints the live registry. Flat/Rough variants exist where noted. | Task id | Terrain | Description | |---|---|---| | `Mjlab-Velocity-{Flat,Rough}-MicroDuck` | flat/rough | **The main task**: walking with velocity commands + head-pose commands | | `Mjlab-VelStand-{Flat,Rough}-MicroDuck` | flat/rough | Walking + fall recovery in one policy | | `Mjlab-StandUp-{Flat,Rough}-MicroDuck` | flat/rough | Stand up from face-down/face-up/sitting, then hold the stand + body-pose control | | `Mjlab-SitStand-{Flat,Rough}-MicroDuck` | flat/rough | Commanded sit ↔ stand in one policy, gently, head commandable | | `Mjlab-GroundPick-{Flat,Rough}-MicroDuck` | flat/rough | Crouch and touch the ground with the mouth tip, return to stand | | `Mjlab-BallKick-Flat-MicroDuck` | flat | Kick a 70 mm / 15 g ball forward (actor is ball-blind) | | `Mjlab-Roulade-Flat-MicroDuck` | flat | Forward roll over the head, land back on the feet | | `Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck-Rollers` | flat | Roller-skate velocity tracking (passive wheels under the feet) | | `Mjlab-Velocity-Swizzle-MicroDuck` | flat | Classic symmetric swizzle skating | | `Mjlab-RollerCrouch-Flat-MicroDuck` | flat | Crouch while gliding on rollers | | `Mjlab-RollerSlope-Flat-MicroDuck` | slope | Glide down slopes on rollers | | `Mjlab-RollerStandUp-Flat-MicroDuck` | flat | Stand up from the ground onto the wheels | | `Mjlab-Spin-Flat-MicroDuck` | flat | Fast spin in place on rollers | At deployment the runtime hot-swaps these policies (walk / recover / trick) behind a shared 61-dimensional observation contract, so any of them can take over the robot at any moment. `scripts/infer_policy.py` rehearses exactly that: ```bash uv run scripts/infer_policy.py --walking walk.onnx --standing stand.onnx \ --sitstand sitstand.onnx --roulade roulade.onnx --new-cmd-obs ``` Keyboard-driven (velocity commands, `G` ground pick, `Y` sit/stand, `R` roulade, `K`/`L` kicks); `--debug`, `--save-csv`, `--record` support sim2real comparisons. The servos are simulated with the same BAM M6 XL330 model the policies are trained against (voltage control + load-dependent friction, via `bam.mujoco.MujocoController`); `--vin` / `--vin-drop-gain` / `--kp-fw` pin the training DR ranges to one value, `--no-bam` falls back to the XML PD actuators. ### Backlash variants Every main task has a **Backlash** twin that trains on a model with ±1° of gear play (2° total) in series with each of the 14 servo joints: insert `-Backlash` before `MicroDuck` in the task id, e.g. `Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-Backlash-MicroDuck`. The backlash is modeled properly for sim2real: each servo gets an unactuated `passive__backlash` hinge, and because the real encoder sits on the output side of the play, both the firmware PD emulation (`BacklashEncoderBamActuator`) and the `joint_pos`/`joint_vel` observations read *through* the backlash (`qpos[servo] + qpos[backlash]`). Observation and action dims are unchanged, so ONNX export and the runtime need no changes. See `src/mjlab_microduck/tasks/backlash.py`. ## Actuator model All tasks use the [BAM](https://github.com/Rhoban/bam) M6 actuator model for the Dynamixel XL330 (voltage control law, back-EMF, Coulomb/Stribeck/load-dependent friction), with per-env domain randomization on battery voltage, voltage sag under load, command delay, and friction magnitude (`FrictionDRBamActuator` in `src/mjlab_microduck/actuator/`). At this scale — tiny servos driving a ~800 g biped — actuator fidelity is most of the sim2real gap, which is why the actuator is modeled down to its voltage control law instead of an ideal PD. ## Robot models MJCF models live in `src/mjlab_microduck/robot/microduck/` and are exported from Onshape with [onshape-to-robot](https://github.com/Rhoban/onshape-to-robot), one `config_mjcf_*.json` per model: | XML | Used by | |---|---| | `robot_walk.xml` | Velocity (stripped trunk/head contacts — falling is cheap) | | `robot_groundcontact.xml` | VelStand, StandUp, SitStand, GroundPick, BallKick, Roulade (curated collision set for the parts that touch the floor — body can physically lie on the ground; formerly `robot_allcollisions.xml`) | | `robot_groundcontact_rollers.xml` | Roller tasks (passive wheels) | | `robot_allcollisions.xml` | True full-collision model — every part has a collision geom. No task uses it yet | | `robot_*_backlash.xml` | Backlash task variants (generated by `add_backlash.py`) | `scene*.xml` files wrap the robots with a floor + keyframes (STAND/SIT/FOLD) for quick viewing and for `infer_policy.py`. ## Project structure ``` src/mjlab_microduck/ ├── robot/ │ ├── microduck/ # MJCF exports, export configs, scenes, add_backlash.py │ └── microduck_constants.py # robot cfgs, HOME frame, BAM actuator cfg ├── actuator/friction_dr_bam.py # BAM + friction DR + backlash encoder feedback ├── tasks/ │ ├── __init__.py # task registration (base + backlash variants) │ ├── mdp.py # rewards, events, observations, custom classes │ ├── backlash.py # make_backlash_variant() env-cfg wrapper │ └── microduck_*_env_cfg.py # one cfg module per task family ├── train_cli.py # `train` script (identical to mjlab's) ├── train_hook.py # intercepts `train ... --hf-jobs` └── hf_jobs.py # Hugging Face Jobs submission ``` Conventions worth knowing: - The observation layout is shared across every policy (61-dim actor obs: 48 proprioception + commands `[twist(3), head_pose(4), body_pose(6)]`), which is what makes runtime policy hot-swapping possible. Envs that don't use a command slot zero-pad it rather than dropping it. - Unactuated joints are all named `passive_*` (roller wheels, backlash hinges); actuators, joint observations and pose rewards select servo joints with `^(?!passive_).*`. - Domain-randomization toggles are `ENABLE_*` booleans at the top of each env cfg file. - Joint layout (14 servos): 0–4 left leg (hip_yaw, hip_roll, hip_pitch, knee, ankle), 5–8 neck/head (neck_pitch, head_pitch, head_yaw, head_roll), 9–13 right leg. - The exporter bakes the observation normalizer into the ONNX graph — always deploy ONNX produced by `scripts/export.py`, never a hand-converted checkpoint, or the policy sees unnormalized observations at runtime. [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) documents the env-building workflow and the reward-design rules learned across the project (also aimed at AI coding agents working in this repo). ## Publishing a policy `uv run publish` puts a policy on the Hugging Face Hub in the shape the robot's daemon loads: one `policy.onnx` with the observation normalizer baked in, a `manifest.json` following schema 2 of the [microduck policy manifest](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck/blob/main/docs/policy-manifest.md), and a README saying how to run it. Anyone with a microduck can then install it with one command, no daemon release needed. ```bash # From a wandb run — exports through the one safe path, then uploads uv run publish --task Mjlab-PoliteBow-Flat-MicroDuck \ --wandb-run-path --checkpoint 3000 \ --repo /microduck-polite-bow --kind episodic --duration-s 4.0 \ --description "Bows from a two-foot stand and comes back up." # From an ONNX you already exported (validated, not re-exported) uv run publish --onnx output.onnx --repo /microduck-flamingo \ --kind perpetual --unwind-s 1.5 --twist-help "[flag, side, 0]" # A new gait for a slot uv run publish --onnx output.onnx --repo /microduck-my-walk --kind perpetual --slot walk # Ship a rollout video too: uploaded as replay.mp4, which the Hub's replay widget plays uv run scripts/render_policy.py output.onnx --seconds 10 --video media/bow.mp4 uv run publish --onnx output.onnx --repo /microduck-bow --kind episodic --duration-s 4.0 \ --video media/bow.mp4 # A remix (warm-started / fine-tuned from someone's published policy): name the parent so the # model card sets `base_model` and the Hub links the two uv run publish --onnx output.onnx --repo /microduck-deep-bow --kind episodic --duration-s 5.0 \ --base-model /microduck-polite-bow # See what would be uploaded without touching the Hub uv run publish --onnx output.onnx --repo /microduck-bow --kind episodic --duration-s 4.0 --dry-run ``` Then on a robot: ```bash sudo robotctl policy add polite-bow /microduck-polite-bow # episodic: length comes from the manifest sudo robotctl policy add flamingo /microduck-flamingo --hold 5 # held pose: you pick how long sudo robotctl policy load walk /microduck-my-walk # gait: into the walk slot robotctl robot do polite-bow ``` What `--kind` means, and what each needs: - **episodic** — runs for `--duration-s` and returns itself to a standing pose (kicks, roulade, a bow). Add `--chain` if holding the button should repeat it. - **perpetual** — runs until told otherwise. Two shapes: - a **gait** (a new walk or stand): add `--slot walk` (or `stand`) and nothing else; the owner installs it with `robotctl policy load walk `. - a **held pose** (the flamingo): give `--unwind-s`, how long the daemon drives the idle twist (`--idle`, zeros by default) before handing back to the gait, so the robot is not let go of on one foot. The owner runs it as a one-shot with `policy add ... --hold `. Before anything is uploaded, `publish` checks the graph is `[1,61] -> [1,14]` (a 51-D legacy policy is refused with a message), runs it on plausible inputs and refuses NaNs or a constant output, fills the `training` block from git and wandb (task, commit, branch, dirty flag, run, checkpoint), and refuses to overwrite an existing `.onnx` in the repo without `--force`. Repos are created private; `--no-private` for public, `--tag v1` to tag the revision. Only constant-command policies are publishable this way. Phase-driven moves (the ground pick) and the posture-flag sit↔stand are driven by the daemon itself and live in the official set, `pollen-robotics/microduck-policies`. ## Tests ```bash uv run --with pytest pytest tests/ ``` CPU-only config-invariant and reward-function regression tests — they lock in joint-index mappings, reward sign conventions, and NaN guards. ## Related projects - [microduck](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck) — the Microduck project home, including the onboard runtime that runs the exported policies - [mjlab](https://github.com/mujocolab/mjlab) — the training framework (MuJoCo Warp + rsl_rl) - [BAM](https://github.com/Rhoban/bam) — better actuator models, by Rhoban ## License The code in this repository is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. See the [LICENSE](LICENSE) file for details. The 3D model files (the `.stl` meshes in `src/mjlab_microduck/robot/microduck/assets/` and `src/mjlab_microduck/robot/xl330_test_bench/assets/`) are licensed under [Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/). See [LICENSE-MODELS.md](LICENSE-MODELS.md) for the exact scope and attribution.

# Microduck 复刻 **简体中文** · [English](README.en.md) 基于 [Pollen Robotics Microduck](https://pollen-robotics.com/microduck/) 的第三方整机复刻项目，提供从采购、打印、装配到标定、控制和训练的资料。 **飞特 HD-1910 版本已完成整机实机验证：站立、行走、前滚翻后起身均已跑通。** 主线使用 **15 颗飞特 HD-1910 舵机**，提供可烧录的**复刻镜像**和 **Microduck Studio 网页中控**，通过手机或电脑浏览器完成配网、标定和遥控。 **首次上手流程已在实机跑通：** 烧录镜像 → 热点配网 → 舵机与 IMU 标定 → 配手柄、测试急停 → 站立行走。[查看实机验证记录](docs/历史更新.md#最近更新) ## 鸭子现在的样子 **2026-10-24 · 实机运动验证通过**：下方两段实拍视频分别展示前滚翻后起身和桌面行走。
前滚翻与起身 桌面行走

动图为无声预览，MP4 保留完整画面和声音。 **[下载镜像](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica/releases/latest)** · **[首次使用指南（PDF / 网页）](docs/上手指南/README.md)** · **[CAD 与打印件](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica-cad)** · **[装配教程](#-装配视频教程)** · **[BOM 采购清单](BOM/README.md)** · **[硬件工程](hardware/README.md)** --- ### 适用版本 - **飞特 HD-1910 + Radxa Zero 3W**：使用本仓复刻镜像和 Studio 网页中控。 - **Dynamixel XL330**：提供对应 CAD 与装配资料，需使用匹配的运行软件。 [选择打印件与采购清单](#打印件与采购清单) · [查看舵机详细对比](docs/执行器选型.md) --- ## 交流群 有人在做同样的事，凑了个微信群一起讨论复刻进度、踩过的坑、元件采购。 下面是**鸭子复刻群 11**的二维码（微信群满 200 人后无法扫码加入）。

### 打印件与采购清单 先按舵机版本选择打印资料，再准备对应的外购件。 | 资料 | 适用版本 | 入口 | |---|---|---| | **打印件与 CAD** | **飞特 HD-1910** | [进入飞特版专区](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica-cad#飞特-hd-1910-打印资料)：打印工程、CAD 源文件和更新说明 | | **打印件与 CAD** | **Dynamixel XL330** | [进入 XL330 版专区](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica-cad#dynamixel-xl330-打印资料)：对应版本的 CAD 源文件与打印说明 | | **装配采购清单** | **飞特 HD-1910** | **[在线预览](BOM/README.md)** · **[下载 Excel](BOM/装配BOM-机械行者Robo-2026-10-23-带采购链接.xlsx)**：机械行者Robo整理，2026-10-23 版，含数量、材料和采购链接 | 两种舵机的配合件不能混用。打印文件的具体版本和更新日期在 CAD 仓库对应专区维护；这份采购清单按飞特方案整理，XL330 的舵机及配套电控需另行核对。 --- ## 现在做到哪了 截至 **2026-10-25**，**飞特版整机复刻、首次上手与实机运动链路已跑通**。下面介绍各部分成果与后续拓展项目，具体测试范围及历史过程见[更新记录](docs/历史更新.md)。 --- ## 💻 软件 · 复刻镜像与 Microduck Studio **复刻镜像 20261023c 已发布。** 烧卡后，用手机或电脑浏览器完成配网、舵机与 IMU 标定、手柄遥控和模型管理，出问题可导出诊断日志。


Studio 界面演示，设备读数为模拟数据

**[下载镜像](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica/releases/latest)** · **[首次使用指南](docs/上手指南/README.md)** · **[Studio 说明](software/studio/README.md)** 镜像免费，仅供个人非商业复刻；各部分许可见发布页。摄像头默认测试源，真实摄像头和 ToF 的验证范围见本版说明。 --- ## 🔧 机械 · 一站式打印与装配 **机械行者Robo持续维护飞特 HD-1910 与 Dynamixel XL330 两套资料。** 模型、打印工程和更新说明集中在 CAD 仓库，按自己的舵机版本选择。 | 需要什么 | 入口 | |---|---| | **一站式打印** | **[拓竹 MakerWorld（飞特版）](https://makerworld.com.cn/zh/models/2963569-microduck#profileId-3478428)** · [Bambu Studio 3MF 工程](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica-cad#打印) | | **模型与打印资料** | **[飞特 HD-1910 专区](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica-cad#飞特-hd-1910-打印资料)** · **[XL330 专区](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica-cad#dynamixel-xl330-打印资料)** | | **装配教程** | **[装配说明书 PDF](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica-cad/blob/master/安装说明书/microduck装配安装说明书.pdf)** · **[分集视频](#-装配视频教程)**；两版按对应结构件装配 | | **采购清单** | **[BOM 在线预览](BOM/README.md)** · **[下载 Excel](BOM/装配BOM-机械行者Robo-2026-10-23-带采购链接.xlsx)**：2026-10-23 飞特版，XL330 的舵机及配套电控需另行核对 | [CAD 仓库与最新发布](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica-cad/releases) · [构建记录](构建日志.md) --- ## 🔌 电气 · 五块电路板 本仓提供总线 IMU 板、舵机总线 HUB 和电池接口板的工程资料；主控采用瑞莎 **Radxa ZERO 3W**，扩展板使用 Pollen Robotics 官方开源的 **RPI Robot HAT**。

🧰 工具 · 烧卡、调试与资料 常用软件和开发工具集中在[工具导航](tools/README.md)，按要做的事选择即可。 | 要做什么 | 工具与入口 | |---|---| | 烧录镜像 | **[Rufus 便携版 EXE](tools/rufus/rufus-4.15p.exe)** · [烧卡说明](tools/rufus/README.md) | | 串口与舵机调试 | **[飞特 FD 与串口助手](tools/飞特/README.md)** · [3D 网页调试台](tools/servo-web/README.md) | | 查飞特资料、接入 SDK | **[官方手册、型号规格书与 SDK](docs/飞特资料/README.md)**，标明官网版本和离线副本日期 | | 测舵机、分析问题 | [HD1910M 测试工具](tools/FeeTech_HD1910M_Servo/README.md) · [STS3215 测试工具](tools/sts3215Servo_testtool/README.md) · [步态分析](tools/gait-analysis/README.md) | --- ## 🦆 鸭友贡献 这个仓库不是一个人写的。合并进来的代码、实测验证过的结论，都记在这儿。 | 谁 | 贡献了什么 | |---|---| | [@yoyojacky](https://github.com/yoyojacky) | **Rust 版飞特舵机测试工具**（[PR #27](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica/pull/27)，已合并）。自己实现的最小 STS/SCS 协议（帧打包、校验和、ping、读写寄存器、状态解析），命令行可以扫描总线（带进度条）、读状态、转到指定位置、单颗测试和批量测试，输出位置偏差、峰值电流、峰值负载、电压温度并判定 PASS/FAIL。台架验收一条命令出汇总表 → [`tools/sts3215Servo_testtool/`](tools/sts3215Servo_testtool/) | | [@Abo1ish](https://github.com/Abo1ish) | **IMU 小板固件 + 调试台姿态显示**（[PR #32](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica/pull/32)，已合并）。给官方没开源的那块 imu_to_dxl 写了 STM32G031 固件底子，在实板上验证过，带主机端测试和一份写清楚边界的 [`VALIDATION.md`](hardware/imu_to_dxl/firmware/VALIDATION.md) → [`hardware/imu_to_dxl/firmware/`](hardware/imu_to_dxl/firmware/)；再用 J-Link 把 IMU 姿态实时读出来并进了网页调试台，3D 鸭子的躯干跟着真板子转（`--imu-jlink`，没板子也能用 `--imu-demo` 先看效果）→ [`tools/servo-web/`](tools/servo-web/) | | 微信群的鸭友 | **Radxa Zero 3W V1.12J 的启动方案**。这批板子（WiFi 换成 AIC8800DS2）光换瑞莎引导还是起不来，他实测出设备树也得换成瑞莎 B1 的：**B1 引导 + B1 DTB + Armbian 6.1.115 内核 + Trixie 系统**，跑通了 → 写进了[踩坑记录](踩坑记录.md#软件)和[镜像使用说明](tools/radxa/镜像使用说明.md#6-如果你的板子不是这一批) | --- ## 鸭友的项目 有些鸭友是自己单独开仓库做的，不在这个仓库里，但跟鸭子直接相关、做得好的，放这儿推一下： | 项目 | 作者 | 做什么的 | |---|---|---| | [microduck-color-studio](https://github.com/LathamZ/microduck-color-studio)（[在线试用](https://lathamz.github.io/microduck-color-studio/)） | [@LathamZ](https://github.com/LathamZ) | **鸭子的 3D 配色工作室，打印前先在网页里把颜色定好。** 70 个零件逐件上色，选材质（PLA / 哑光 / PETG / 金属 / 碳纤 / TPU）和灯光看效果；填上自己手里有哪些耗材，它按库存推荐配色（只用已有 / 补一色 / 丙烯点缀）。还能导入自己的 3MF（比如飞特版），导出**带颜色的多盘 3MF** 和按件拆好的 STL，拓竹 P1S / A1 mini / H2D 有预设。中英文界面，手机上也能看 | | [MICDUCK_FTHD1901_REBUILD](https://github.com/fengj4780-sudo/MICDUCK_FTHD1901_REBUILD) | [@fengj4780-sudo](https://github.com/fengj4780-sudo) | **飞特版结构改进 + 可选 CNC 加强件。** 在我们的[可编辑 SolidWorks 图纸](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica-cad)基础上接着改：适配飞特舵机（他仓库里写作 HD1901，零件文件用的是 HD-1910-C001），加强了薄弱件，修了装配干涉和几个破损的模型。腿部 **5 个零件可以换成 CNC 件**让受力更合理（还在打样测试，他估算 5 件含运费约 45 元）；不做 CNC 直接打印也行，强度也比原版好。附一键打印的 3MF（拓竹 H2D、0.4 mm、5 盘）和改好的 SolidWorks 图纸 | | [Microduck-kissqy](https://github.com/kissqy/Microduck-kissqy) | [@kissqy](https://github.com/kissqy) | **飞特 HD1910 的训练流程与控制实现参考。** 提供训练中控、训练环境准备与任务管理说明、ONNX 模型导出，以及机器人中控、固件和演示视频；算法部分的具体训练流程推荐参考这个项目 | 做了跟鸭子有关的项目（工具、教程、改装、策略……），开 issue 贴个链接，我们加进来。 想加进来：直接开 [issue](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica/issues) 或提 PR。 硬件、固件、算法、文档、实测数据都算 —— **实测数据尤其欢迎**，这个仓库的规矩是结论如实记录，无论正反。 --- ## 资料导航 路径相对于本仓库根目录；机械 CAD 在独立仓库维护。 | 项目 | 仓库位置 | 说明与入口 | |---|---|---| | 使用与装配 | [CAD 仓库](https://github.com/fanhao375/microduck-replica-cad) · [BOM/](BOM/README.md) | [首次使用指南](docs/上手指南/README.md) · [采购清单](BOM/README.md) · [装配视频](#-装配视频教程) | | 软件与镜像 | [software/](software/README.md) | [Studio 中控](software/studio/README.md) · [镜像构建](software/image/README.md) | | 训练平台与工程 | [software/training-studio/](software/training-studio/README.md)
[software/training/](software/training/README.md) | 网页训练工作台、仿真环境与模型导出 | | 电气与固件 | [hardware/](hardware/README.md) | [电路板工程](hardware/README.md) · [IMU 固件](hardware/imu_to_dxl/README.md) | | 调试与分析工具 | [tools/](tools/README.md) | [工具导航](tools/README.md) · 烧卡、串口调试、飞特资料和分析脚本 | | 文档与记录 | [docs/](docs/README.md) | [完整文档导航](docs/README.md) · [踩坑](踩坑记录.md) · [调试](调试记录.md) · [构建](构建日志.md) | | 历史与社区 | [docs/](docs/README.md#深入研究与归档) | [官方更新跟踪](docs/官方更新跟踪.md) · [历史更新](docs/历史更新.md) · [社区贡献](docs/社区贡献.md) | --- ## 许可与来源 代码、仿真素材和镜像内模型分别适用各自许可，详见[许可与署名](NOTICE.md)及[模型使用条款](software/image/overlay/usr/share/doc/microduck/模型说明.txt)。**复刻镜像仅供个人非商业复刻，不得随收费产品分发。** 本项目与 Pollen Robotics 无隶属关系，未获其背书。 ### ❤️ 支持作者 从装配、调试到软件和文档，这个项目是靠一次次尝试积累起来的。如果这些资料和工具帮到了你，欢迎点个 Star ⭐、反馈问题或分享复刻经验；也可以自愿打赏，请作者喝杯咖啡，支持项目继续维护。感谢每一位鸭友的支持。

# Duck on Desk

English | [简体中文](README.zh-CN.md)

A physics-driven 3D Microduck that lives on your desktop and reacts to your AI coding agents — Claude Code, Codex CLI, Pi and opencode. Thinking when you prompt, walking when tools run, quacking at you when an agent needs approval, sulking on errors, sleeping when you step away.

> AGPL-3.0 derivative of [Clawd on Desk](https://github.com/rullerzhou-afk/clawd-on-desk) (baseline `5ca26b5c`). The duck is the official Pollen Robotics Microduck simulator rig, MuJoCo physics and RL walking policies, not pre-baked animation. See `NOTICE.md`.

## Demo

![Duck on Desk: skins, roller skates and stilts on the desktop](docs/media/demo.gif)

[Full demo with sound (80 s, MP4)](https://github.com/Happenmass/duck-on-desk/releases/latest/download/duck-on-desk-demo.mp4)

## Install

Prebuilt apps are on the [Releases](https://github.com/Happenmass/duck-on-desk/releases) page:

- **macOS**: `Duck-on-Desk-<version>-arm64.dmg` (Apple Silicon) or `-x64.dmg` (Intel). The build is unsigned, so after dragging it to Applications run once:
  `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/Duck on Desk.app"`
- **Windows**: `Duck-on-Desk-Setup-<version>-x64.exe` or `-arm64.exe` (SmartScreen: More info → Run anyway).

Everything the duck needs is inside the app, including the RL policies (see `NOTICE.md` for their sources); nothing is downloaded at runtime. Launch, open the tray menu → Settings → Agents, and install the hooks for Claude Code, Codex, Pi or opencode.

## Developer mode and training

Enable **Settings → About → Developer mode** to open the separate 3D robot laboratory. Inspect or control 14 joints, edit rewards and policy networks, run PPO training, evaluate, export ONNX, apply a policy to the desktop pet, and roll back.

The Agents page can install Robot Lab MCP for Claude Code, Codex CLI and OpenCode so coding agents can read API docs, write scripts and manage training. Walking training embeds the official mjlab / microduck_rl environment unchanged (the app clones the pinned commit and runs `uv sync`, so Git is required); on Apple Silicon physics runs on the CPU with the network on MPS, on NVIDIA it uses CUDA. MPS has been tested; CUDA awaits NVIDIA hardware verification. This first version trains the standard feet on flat ground. See [Robot Lab instructions](mcp/robot-lab/README.md).

## Roller skates

The tray menu's **Locomotion** entry switches the duck between its feet and the
official roller-skate variant: the shipped `BEST_roller` policy drives four
passive wheels (push, coast, brake) and `BEST_roller_crouch` is its crouch-glide
trick, which the duck performs whenever it would otherwise peck. Both policies
ship with the app like the walking ones. The policy was
trained without a turning demand, so on skates the duck is steered by rotating
its body directly, inside a wider ±80° camera-facing cone; a little bearing drag
on the wheels keeps the glide at a desktop pace. It cannot sit, and free roam
slides the window by the distance actually rolled.

## Stilts (experimental)

The tray menu's **Stilts** entry puts the duck on the community stilt policies
(`HannesVonEssen/microduck-stilts`, trained in `Vottivott/microduck-playground`).
They ship with the app too (Apache-2.0).

Heights 10–25 cm are the printable ones; 50 cm–2 m are simulation-only. On
stilts the duck walks and turns but does not sit, peck or get up on its own
(a fallen duck is stood back up), and the servo gains are doubled: like every Microduck policy they were trained
against the BAM servo model, and unlike the official ones they do not tolerate
the plain MJCF position actuators this simulator runs.

## Agents
| Agent | Integration | States | Permission bubble |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | command hooks in `~/.claude/settings.json` + HTTP `PermissionRequest` hook | all | yes |
| Codex CLI | official hooks in `~/.codex/hooks.json`, JSONL polling fallback | all | yes |
| opencode | plugin in `~/.config/opencode/` | all | yes (bridge) |
| Pi | global extension in `~/.pi/agent/extensions/duck-on-desk` | state-only | no (by design) |

## How states become duck behaviour
See `docs/guides/state-mapping.md`.

## Skins
Tray → Skin: Cream, Graphite, Lavender, Sky (the four real Microduck colourways). Voices follow the skin.

## Development
`npm ci && npm run setup:models && npm start` (`setup:models` fetches the policies into your Hugging Face cache once) · `npm test` · `npm run build:mac` / `npm run build:win:all`

## Acknowledgements

- [Clawd on Desk](https://github.com/rullerzhou-afk/clawd-on-desk) by rullerzhou-afk and contributors (AGPL-3.0): the desktop-pet shell, agent integrations, permission bubbles and settings this project is derived from (baseline commit `5ca26b5c`).
- [Microduck](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck) by Pollen Robotics (Apache-2.0): the tiny biped duck robot itself; [microduck_rl](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck_rl): the RL training environments behind the walking, sitting, ground-pick and roller policies; and the [Microduck simulator Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/pollen-robotics/microduck-simulator): the 3D rig, MJCF, voices and the policies this duck runs (3D assets and voices are non-commercial, see `NOTICE.md`).
- [microduck-playground](https://github.com/Vottivott/microduck-playground) by Vottivott (Apache-2.0) and the [microduck-stilts](https://huggingface.co/HannesVonEssen/microduck-stilts) weights by HannesVonEssen: the community stilt training and policies.
- The servo steps and landings are cut from "Small servo (arduino)" by gpag1 (CC0, on [freesound](https://freesound.org/people/gpag1/sounds/520514/)); the notification sound is CC0 by iut_Paris8 on freesound; agent icons come from [LobeHub Icons](https://lobehub.com/icons).
- The demo video's music is "Fluffing a Duck" by Kevin MacLeod ([incompetech.com](https://incompetech.com)), licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
